rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say night and day alternate so worship or good deeds missed in one can be accomplished during the other.
rows.anchor: whatever one could not accomplish (by way of worship or good deeds) in the day one could accomplish at night, and vice versa (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr cites a ḥadīth in which God extends His Hand by night to forgive daytime sin and by day to forgive nighttime sin.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathīr mentions the ḥadīth: “God, glorified and resplendent is He, extends His Hand by night

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some understand khilfah as opposition: night and day are opposites, one dark and the other light.
rows.anchor: that is, one dark and the other light (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation of night and day is a Quranic sign of God, as is the passage of day into night and night into day.
rows.anchor: The alternation of the night and day is cited in the Quran as a sign of God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The verse concerns reflecting on or giving thanks for the blessings of day and night.
rows.anchor: One desires to reflect on or desires to be thankful for the blessings of the day and night (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: Commentators agree that al-Rūm was revealed in the Makkan period.
rows.anchor: A ll commentators agree that al-Rūm was revealed

rows.speaker: Aj, Āl
rows.claim: Aj and Āl maintain that verse 17 is Madinan.
rows.anchor: some maintain that v. 17 is from the Madinan period (Aj, Āl)

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: IJ maintains that verses 27–28 are Madinan.
rows.anchor: others maintain that vv. 27–28 are from the Madinan period (IJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the defeat of the Byzantines, or Romans, mentioned in verse 2.
rows.anchor: sūrah takes its name from

rows.speaker: Āl, Sy
rows.claim: Some link the promise of Byzantine victory to the preceding sūrah’s promise that God guides those who strive for His sake.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, God’s promise that the Byzantines would prevail after having been defeated (v. 3) follows upon the last verse of the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Others link the sūrahs through the promise that God is with the virtuous and that believers will rejoice in His Help.
rows.anchor: the promise in vv. 4–5 that on that day the believers shall rejoice in God’s Help (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening prediction of Byzantine victory leads to criticism of disbelievers for failing to reflect on God’s signs.
rows.anchor: From the mention of the battle between the Sassanids and the Byzantines and the prediction of the eventual victory of the Byzantines (vv. 2–6) followed by a criticism of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion turns from the disbelievers’ failure to reflect to the different ends of believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: the sūrah proceeds to a discussion of the disparate ends of believers and disbelievers (vv. 10–16)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s central theme is the abundance of signs in creation and many people’s inability to understand them because they follow caprice rather than knowledge.
rows.anchor: the sūrah’s central theme, the abundance of signs of God in the created order and the inability of many human beings to understand them, because they follow caprice rather than knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 30–34 contrast those who follow the upright religion, beginning with human beings’ primordial fiṭrah, with those who split religion into factions.
rows.anchor: Beginning with a reference to the original or primordial nature of human beings, the fiṭrah, in one of the Quran’s more famous verses (v. 30), vv. 30–34 contrast those who follow the upright religion with those who divide religion into factions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After challenging disbelievers to substantiate their claims, the sūrah treats kinship rights, just use of wealth, human life phases, and corruption.
rows.anchor: Challenging the disbelievers to bring something to substantiate their claims (v. 35), the sūrah then touches upon several broader Quranic themes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After calling people to upright religion, the sūrah contrasts believers and disbelievers and returns to reflection on God’s signs.
rows.anchor: After calling again to the upright religion (vv. 43), al-Rūm returns to the contrast between the believers and disbelievers (vv. 44–45), which leads into another extended passage on its central theme, the importance of reflecting upon God’s signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reminder that the Prophet cannot guide those God has not guided is followed by the guilty’s difficulties at Judgment.
rows.anchor: A reminder of the Prophet’s inability to guide those whom God has not guided (vv. 52–54) is then followed by a discussion of the difficulties that will confront the guilty upon the Hour of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes by recalling that disbelievers’ hearts are sealed and urging steadfastness when facing them.
rows.anchor: The sūrah concludes with a reminder that their hearts are sealed (v. 59) and that one must thus remain steadfast when confronted by them (v. 60).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses the plural “winds” ten times, each time expressing God’s mercy, including the cited passages.
rows.anchor: Winds appears in the plural form ten times in the Quran, and each time it expresses God’s Mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular “wind” usually conveys God’s wrath and punishment.
rows.anchor: In contrast, when wind occurs in the singular, it is usually used to convey God’s Wrath and Punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinction may reflect a view that south, east, and north winds bring mercy, while the west wind brings punishment and destruction.
rows.anchor: the winds of the south, east, and north are all said to bring mercy; only the west wind is said to bring punishment and destruction

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Kisaf, translated “fragments,” can also mean “piled up.”
rows.anchor: Fragments renders kisaf, which could also mean “piled up” (IK).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Those receiving rain may have despaired from need before the rain relieved them.
rows.anchor: The people to whom the rain came may have been in despair because they were in need, and the rain relieved their despair (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, people may have feared a violent storm when the winds arose, then felt relief when only rain came.
rows.anchor: in despair when the winds first arose, thinking that a violent storm was coming

rows.speaker: Aj, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The initial weakness may refer to humanity’s creation from a base fluid.

rows.speaker: Aj, Q, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, the initial weakness may refer to a child’s weakness at the beginning of life.
rows.anchor: or to the weakness of a child at the beginning of life (Aj, Q, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strength after initial weakness refers to youth and maturity, followed by decline in old age.
rows.anchor: Strength then refers to the period of youth and maturity, followed by the period of decline in old age.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran 22:5 presents all earthly life stages, from conception to old age, as signs of God’s Power.
rows.anchor: where all of the stages of earthly life from conception to old age are cited as signs of God’s Power

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also speaks of regression in creation and return to the weakest age, when people may know nothing after having had knowledge.
rows.anchor: 36:68, which speaks of those whom God causes to regress in creation

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The guilty’s claim that they tarried an hour may mean their experience of the period in the grave before Resurrection.
rows.anchor: either to their experience of the period in the grave before the Day of Resurrection or to their period of time on earth (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, the claim may refer to their earthly lifetime, which seems like an hour or less beside the Hereafter’s eternity.
rows.anchor: either to their experience of the period in the grave before the Day of Resurrection or to their period of time on earth (Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The guilty may make the claim in ignorance or to argue that the evidence against them is insufficient.
rows.anchor: Their claim may be made in ignorance or in order to argue that there is not enough proof against them (IK).

rows.speaker: Iṣ
rows.claim: Yuʾfakū literally means “turned away” and connotes a negative turning from truth toward falsehood, such as lying or ugly deeds.
rows.anchor: from truth toward falsehood—turning from telling the truth to lying or from beautiful actions to ugly ones (Iṣ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Yuʾfakū can also mean “thus were they deluded,” describing their mistaken view of this world’s relation to the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: “thus were they deluded” (Z) in their understanding of the relationship of this world to the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fāṭir is a Makkan sūrah reportedly revealed just after al-Furqān, Sūrah 25.
rows.anchor: A Makkan sūrah, Fāṭir was reportedly revealed immediately after Sūrah 25, al-Furqān

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Ṭs assigns verses 27 and 32 to the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: According to some, vv. 27 and 32 are from the Madinan period (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Āl assigns verses 29 and 32 to the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: while others maintain that vv. 29 and 32 are Madinan (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for God as Originator of the heavens and earth in verse 1; it is also often called al-Malāʾikah, “The Angels.”
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the reference to God as the Originator of the heavens and the earth in v. 1, but is often known as al-Malāʾikah, “The Angels”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 1 gives the Quran’s only description of some aspects of the angels’ physical appearance.
rows.anchor: since v. 1 provides the only description of some aspects of the angels’ physical appearance in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s main focus is God’s oneness as the sole Creator and Sustainer, contrasting divine Power with claims made for idols.
rows.anchor: The main focus of the sūrah is upon the Oneness of God as the only Creator and Sustainer of existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of Satan as Deluder and enemy leads into a contrast between believers and disbelievers, including a poetic contrast in verses 19–22.
rows.anchor: A discussion of Satan as the Deluder and enemy (vv. 5–8) leads into the other major theme of this sūrah, the contrast between the believers and the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 19–22 offer one of the Quran’s most poetic contrasts between believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: vv. 19–22 provide one of the most poetic contrasts between the two groups

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The longest comparison of believers and disbelievers in verses 29–39 leads into a final contrast between God’s Power and idols, then the outcomes of disbelief.
rows.anchor: The longest comparison between the two groups (vv. 29–39), followed by a final contrast between the Power of God and that of the idols (vv. 40–41), segues into a final passage on the nature of disbelief and the ends to which it leads (vv. 42–45)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After witnessing the Resurrection and Judgment they denied and admitting sin, disbelievers seek reprieve and promise righteousness, as in their plea to be sent back.
rows.anchor: Having witnessed the realities of Resurrection and Judgment that they had denied (see 32:12; 19:38) and been made to admit their sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warners sent to them and their lifetime to reflect were already a reprieve; repentance is not accepted once death confronts an evildoer or disbeliever.
rows.anchor: the warners who had been sent to them and the opportunity to reflect throughout their life constitute such a reprieve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God rejects requests for return because even if sent back, wrongdoers would again do what they had been forbidden.
rows.anchor: God thus denies all such requests, because even if they were sent back, they would return to the very thing they had been forbidden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wrongdoers have no helpers because they turned away from God and the help He sent them during worldly life.
rows.anchor: because they turned away from God and the help that He sent them during their life in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This and related verses can be read as part of an extended discourse between God and Hell’s inhabitants.
rows.anchor: this and other verses can be seen as part of an extended discourse between God and the denizens of Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God made Adam a vicegerent, He appoints all humanity as vicegerents upon earth.
rows.anchor: Just as God created Adam as a vicegerent upon the earth (2:30), so too has God appointed all human beings as vicegerents upon the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity’s vicegerency connects to the reminder that God made the earth’s contents subservient to people.
rows.anchor: Thus humanity is asked, Hast thou not considered that God has made whatsoever is on the earth subservient unto you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelief harms only its holder and relates to the principle that no one bears another’s burden, because no one carries another’s disbelief.
rows.anchor: since no one can carry the burden of another’s disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelief also rejects humanity’s true nature and responsibility toward God, given its vicegerent role.
rows.anchor: they reject their true nature and responsibility toward God

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The longer disbelievers persist, the more they will lose on the Day of Resurrection; this explains their growing odium.
rows.anchor: the longer they persist in their disbelief, the more they will lose on the Day of Resurrection (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages show messengers’ calls increasing disbelievers’ opposition and other negative reactions.
rows.anchor: For other passages where the call of God’s messengers increases disbelievers in opposition and other negative reactions
